proposed.name: Golden Copy Tiebreaker
proposed.one_liner: When two reference-data vendors disagree about a security before the open, Exa finds the issuer's own announcement, dated and cited, and fills in a vendor-escalation ticket in under 20 seconds.
proposed.customer: A mid-size US asset manager (assume $50B to $300B AUM, equities plus investment-grade credit). It runs a vendor OMS on a golden-copy security master built from two or more licensed reference-data feeds plus custodian files. Economic buyer: Head of Investment Operations or Data Governance. Team: 5 to 15 security master and trade support analysts, plus a small data engineering group that owns the exception pipeline and would own the Exa integration. The size and team are assumptions for the framing. No real firm is named, and it is not a former AJ client.
proposed.end_user: Security master analyst (also called reference data or trade support analyst). From about 7 AM they work the exception queue produced by the overnight golden-copy build and the custodian reconciliation. It has to be clear before the 9:30 open, so that pre-trade compliance and order routing use the right CUSIP, share count and bond status. During the day they take calls when an order rejects on an unknown identifier or a compliance rule fires unexpectedly, and they open tickets with whichever data vendor has the wrong value. Late in the day they chase allocation and DTCC CTM mismatches that trace back to the same bad data.
proposed.problem: The decision: which vendor's value is right, and since when. A real example from this month: Lument Finance Trust (NYSE: LFT) announced a 1-for-10 reverse split on Aug 13, 2026 and completed it after the close on Sep 9. From Sep 10 it trades under new CUSIP 55025L306, with shares outstanding cut from 52,564,062 to about 5,256,400. If one feed updates and another lags, the golden copy ends up with two CUSIPs and a share count that is 10x off. Three things then break: the position no longer matches the custodian, an order on the old CUSIP can reject at the broker, and any ownership-limit compliance rule that divides by shares outstanding runs on the wrong denominator. Bonds do the same thing when an issuer calls notes early. Bank of America redeemed CUSIP 06051GLX5 on Sep 15, 2026, and Fifth Third announced on Sep 24 that CUSIP 316773 DD9 will be redeemed Nov 1, 2026. A feed that misses the call leaves a live position in a bond that no longer exists. Today the analyst searches Google, wades through re-posts, opens EDGAR, finds the issuer's release, compares dates by eye and types the ticket. Assume 20 to 30 minutes per exception. What goes wrong: breaks that slip past the open become rejected or busted trades and wrong compliance results, and vendor escalations sent without evidence bounce back.
proposed.why_outside_web_content: Licensed reference data (Bloomberg, LSEG/Refinitiv, ICE) is the system of record and stays that way. In this workflow those feeds are the two values that disagree, so neither one can settle the dispute. The tiebreaker is a primary source: the issuer's press release, its 8-K, or the exchange notice, all on the public web. Google gets a person there slowly, but it has three problems here. First, you cannot pin it to a primary-source domain list and a date window around the break. Second, it mixes in re-posts: even an unfiltered Exa query for the BAC redemption returned investingnews.com, marketscreener.com and scanx.trade copies next to the issuer's page. Third, it returns links, not fields with a citation for each field that can go straight into a ticket. There is also no sanctioned Google API to build on: the Custom Search JSON API is closed to new customers and ends Jan 1, 2027, and Bing's search API was retired in Aug 2025 (per exa-gtm-competitors.md). Exa is the corroboration layer for exceptions only, not a replacement for the licensed feed.
exa_calls: Call 1, evidence search (live, about 1 s, $0.007). Endpoint: POST /search. Parameters: query 'Issuer press release or SEC filing announcing that Lument Finance Trust (NYSE: LFT) common stock will trade under a new CUSIP after a reverse stock split, with the effective date and shares outstanding'; type 'auto'; numResults 10; includeDomains ['sec.gov','prnewswire.com','businesswire.com','globenewswire.com','accessnewswire.com','nasdaq.com/press-release','nyse.com','nasdaqtrader.com']; startPublishedDate '2026-06-12T00:00:00Z' (break date minus 90 days); endPublishedDate = today; contents {highlights: {query: 'effective date, new CUSIP, split ratio, shares outstanding, redemption date, redemption price', maxCharacters: 800}}. Why each choice: auto is the balanced default and a person is waiting. The query describes the ideal page rather than listing keywords. The domain list holds primary sources only and is set in code from config, never by a model; that is what drops the re-posts. The date window brackets the break, so an older split at the same issuer cannot win. Highlights, because the analyst scans the list and the next call reads excerpts, not whole pages. No maxAgeHours: a press release does not change after publication, so forcing a live crawl only adds latency. Verified: a close variant of this filter set, run through Exa's keyless MCP, returned the Sep 9 completion notice and the Aug 13 announcement on prnewswire.com.

Call 2, evidence packet (live, about 6 to 17 s, $0.012). Endpoint: POST /search. Parameters: type 'deep'; the same includeDomains and dates; query 'Lument Finance Trust (NYSE: LFT) common stock: what corporate action changed its CUSIP and shares outstanding in September 2026? Vendor A shows CUSIP 55025L306 and about 5.26 million shares; Vendor B shows the pre-split CUSIP and 52.56 million shares.'; additionalQueries ['LFT 1-for-10 reverse stock split new CUSIP 55025L306', 'Lument Finance Trust 8-K reverse stock split effective time'] (kept at 2, under exa-py's documented max of 5); systemPrompt 'You are verifying a security master exception for an investment operations team. Use only issuer press releases, SEC filings and exchange notices. When a later notice from the issuer updates an earlier one, use the later one. If a field is not stated in a source, answer not stated; never infer.'; outputSchema {type:'object', required:[all 8], properties: event_type (enum: reverse split, forward split, ticker change, name change, merger, redemption, tender, delisting, other), announced_date, effective_date, field_changed, old_value, new_value, terms, vendor_that_matches (enum: Vendor A, Vendor B, neither, cannot tell)}. That is 8 properties at one level, inside the 10-property limit. contents {highlights: true}. Why deep: more than 3 fields plus a judgment across two sources is where the docs recommend deep types. output.content holds the fields. output.grounding gives each field (for example effective_date) its citations and a low, medium or high confidence, so the schema itself carries no citation or confidence fields. The app shows every field with its link and confidence, and builds the ticket text only from grounded fields.

Call 3, the same two calls on a bond row. Query 'Issuer press release announcing redemption of Bank of America Floating Rate Senior Notes due September 2027, CUSIP 06051GLX5, with redemption date and redemption price'. includeDomains adds 'newsroom.bankofamerica.com' (the issuer IR site, taken from the golden copy's issuer record when it has one). Why: shows that the same pattern generalizes from equity corporate actions to fixed-income calls with a config change and no new code. Verified: the keyless MCP returned the BAC newsroom release of Sep 4 at the top.

Optional call 4, audit trail with Snapshot (pre-run, not live). Endpoint: POST /contents. Parameters: urls ['https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lument-finance-trust-announces-completion-of-reverse-stock-split-302874329.html']; snapshotAsOf '2026-09-10T13:30:00Z'; highlights {query: 'new CUSIP effective date'}. Content options sit at the top level on /contents, not inside a contents wrapper. Why: when a vendor pushes back, this returns the page as Exa stored it at the open on the effective date, which proves the fact was public before the break. Limits: rolling 5-month window, 'after 100 requests, talk to sales', cannot be combined with maxAgeHours, and a CONTENT_NOT_CACHED status is possible. So it is shown from cache as a 'where this goes next' feature.

Not used, on purpose. /answer: not covered by Zero Data Retention, and holdings appear in these queries. findSimilar: deprecated. livecrawl: replaced by maxAgeHours. Agent and Websets: async or a separate plan, and a single exception does not need them. Reliability: every call goes through the existing C:\Users\ajwal\Documents\exa-demo\app\exa_client.py. It times out deep calls at 45 s, retries 429 and 503 with Retry-After capped at 5 s, logs requestId and costDollars, and falls back to the saved response with the failure reason shown on screen.

Screen 4, point-in-time timeline (1 min). Three dots: announced Aug 13, effective Sep 10, and the date the stale vendor still disagreed. Say: 'In my paper-trading research system the hardest rule was to use only what was knowable on the date. Ops has the same question: when could we have known?'

Slide 3, business impact and POC (5 min). Walk through the arithmetic and the success criteria below, then ask two discovery questions back: 'How many exceptions a day need an outside check?' and 'Which incident last quarter traced back to reference data?'
proposed.business_impact: Assumptions to confirm in discovery: 20 exceptions a day need an outside check; each takes 25 minutes by hand today and 5 minutes to review an Exa packet; 250 trading days; $100 an hour loaded analyst cost. Time saved: 20 x 20 minutes = 400 minutes a day, about 6.7 hours. Over 250 days that is about 1,670 hours a year, close to one full-time analyst, or about $167K. Exa cost at list: one auto search ($0.007) plus one deep search ($0.012) = $0.019 per exception. At 5,000 exceptions a year that is about $95, and even with retries and extra results it stays under $1,000 before enterprise terms. ZDR pricing is contractual, so do not quote it. The time saving is the floor. The bigger number is avoided rejected or busted trades and wrong compliance results, which the customer should price from its own incident log. POC (2 weeks, 2 analysts): an eval set of 50 to 100 exceptions resolved in the last 90 days, where the right answer is already known. Success means all of these: the primary source is in the top 10 results for at least 90 percent; effective date and new value match the resolution for at least 95 percent of those; no more than 1 high-confidence wrong field across the set; median time to packet under 20 seconds. Then a one-week shadow run where analysts log handling time with and without the packet, targeting at least a 50 percent cut. The eval costs about $2 in Exa credits, well inside the free tier.
proposed.aj_credibility: Strong: he supported the people who do this job. Charles River Development, Nov 2023 to Apr 2026 (two and a half years), Senior Associate FIX Analyst: he triaged security reference data problems with the data services team. They taught him what a golden-copy security is and how to tell which provider caused a break, and he saw bad reference data bust trades. He also handled allocations and DTCC CTM. Adroit, Apr to Aug 2026, Integration Specialist: every client sent a security master in its own undocumented dialect; he built the pre-go-live harness that lists every unmapped value instead of letting it silently default, and worked with the Charles River REST APIs for security reference data and pre-trade compliance. His paper-trading research system gives him the announced vs effective vs knowable date discipline. Three follow-ups he can answer without bluffing: (1) How does the analyst find out? Morning recon against the custodian, a pre-trade compliance fail, a broker reject on an unknown identifier, a CTM mismatch. (2) What decides which vendor wins in the golden copy? Precedence rules by field and the escalation to the data vendor. (3) What happens downstream if it is not fixed by the open? Honest boundary: he saw this from the vendor side and never sat in an asset manager's security master seat. So he says 'the ops teams I supported at Charles River', never names clients, and never claims volumes he did not measure.
proposed.overlap_with_exa_gallery: Low. The nearest are Adverse Media (one deep search per risk topic on a named company, for KYC), Company Enrichment, and Market Monitor (company-level fields and event streams). None of them works at the instrument level (CUSIP, share count, note redemption), none settles a disagreement between two data vendors, and none produces an ops ticket. exa-demos-customers.md lists buy-side investment operations and corporate-action validation as a gap with no public demo. It also stays clear of the mizuho-applet stock-sentiment idea. The framing risk is drifting into 'company news search', so every screen should stay anchored to the exception row and the ticket.
risks: Content check done 2026-09-29. WebSearch and WebFetch on prnewswire.com, globenewswire.com, nasdaq.com/press-release, sec.gov (the LFT 8-K exhibit and Fifth Third's Sep 24 8-K) and newsroom.bankofamerica.com. Also nine probe searches through Exa's public keyless MCP endpoint (mcp.exa.ai, tool web_search_advanced_exa, no account or key). Under the includeDomains and date filters above they returned the LFT releases, ten September note redemptions and ten late-September reverse-split releases. The REST API itself was not called, because there is no key yet.

publishedDate is an estimate. Verizon's release (URL dated 2026/08/20, text says Aug. 20) came back with publishedDate 2026-09-21. Always show the date extracted from the text with its grounding, and say this out loud as a known limit rather than letting Ryan find it.

Holdings in queries reveal positions. Production needs a Zero Data Retention enterprise team, and the free tier is not ZDR, so the demo uses only public September examples. /answer is avoided deliberately because ZDR does not cover it.
Likely objection: 'our vendor already sends corporate actions.' The answer: Exa is only for exceptions where the licensed feeds disagree or lag. Do not pitch replacing the feed.
Coverage not checked: small-issuer IR sites, non-US issuers, municipal bonds (MSRB EMMA) and structured products. Keep the demo to US equities and corporate bonds, and say that plainly.
Untested until a key exists: enum support inside /search outputSchema and real deep latency. Test on Wednesday. The fallbacks are a plain string field and the cached run.
Volumes, minutes and $100 an hour are assumptions, not data. Label them as discovery placeholders on the slide.
Snapshot is optional only: 5-month window, 100 requests before a sales conversation, possible CONTENT_NOT_CACHED, and no maxAgeHours.

Possible talking point, not a risk (verify first and frame it as a question): the hosted MCP reported server version 3.2.1 on initialize, and its web_search_advanced_exa tool still lists startCrawlDate and endCrawlDate, includeText and excludeText, and the pdf and github categories, which the API reference marks as ignored or deprecated. proposed.name: Cutover Radar
proposed.one_liner: Reads every exchange, trade-reporting and clearing notice on a domain list the customer owns, turns each into a dated, cited change row (go-live, first test date, FIX impact) and maps it to the clients it will break. The connectivity team then schedules the certification instead of learning about the change from rejects.
proposed.customer: A trading-technology vendor (OMS, EMS or OEMS) whose FIX network connects a few hundred buy-side and broker clients to brokers, exchanges, trade-reporting facilities and clearing. Economic buyer: Head of Client Connectivity or FIX Onboarding. Expansion buyer: the product manager for the client portal, who could ship the feed to every client. Team: 10 to 30 connectivity analysts working a ticket queue with a weekend on-call rotation, plus the engineers who own the FIX engine and its routing configuration. The size is an assumption. No real firm is named, and it is not a former AJ client.
proposed.end_user: FIX connectivity analyst, the job family AJ held at Charles River. Their day: a queue of new broker and venue connections, certifications and client reject tickets. They read spec and notice updates and decide which clients each one touches. They book test windows and weekend production-verification slots with venues, explain changes to a client's IT team, and cover on-call for dropped sessions and sequence-number problems.
proposed.problem: The decision: which of this quarter's changes hit which clients, and what must be tested by when. Q4 2026 is stacked (all dates from the primary notices). US equities move to 23/5 trading on Dec 6, 2026. Nasdaq opened its test facility for the FINRA/Nasdaq TRF 23/5 changes on Sep 28, with weekend UAT dates of Oct 2, 16 and 30, Nov 6 and 20, and Dec 4 (Equity Trader Alert 2026-50). Cboe's EDGX overnight FAQ, current as of Sep 23, says there are no FIX or BOE protocol changes, but it redefines DAY, GTD and GTX time-in-force to start at 9:00 PM, with test symbols from Nov 9. FINRA's ORF final cutover to Native FIX is Dec 11, 2026, and FINRA expects legacy TRACE FIX to end 'late 4th Quarter 2026'. BrokerTec (CME) flags Nov 2 for bilateral Treasury cash participants to move to central clearing, ahead of the SEC's Dec 31, 2026 cash clearing date. Each of these lives on a separate venue, SRO or clearing site, some as PDFs, and analysts track them by hand from mailing lists and bookmarks. The dangerous ones either change meaning without changing a tag (an OMS that expires DAY orders at the 4 PM close gets the Cboe change wrong) or switch off old sessions on a fixed date (the ORF legacy ports). What goes wrong: rejects or failed sessions on cutover weekend, late trade reports for broker clients, emergency certifications, client escalations and SLA credits. Assume each analyst spends about 3 hours a week just scanning.
proposed.why_outside_web_content: Market-data vendors such as Bloomberg and LSEG/Refinitiv sell prices, reference data and news. News covers the headline (23/5 is coming) but not the working detail a connectivity team acts on: the test-facility calendar, the port request form, the rule on the new Native FIX sessions that MsgSeqNum resets to 1 at each day's logon, or the time-in-force redefinition. That detail sits on nasdaqtrader.com, cboe.com, finra.org, nyse.com, dtcc.com and cmegroup.com, and no licensed feed normalizes it into dated fields. Google can find any one notice for someone who already knows it exists. But no Google API searches only a customer's 40-site list inside a date window and returns fields with a citation for each (the Custom Search JSON API is closed to new customers and ends Jan 1, 2027; Bing's API was retired Aug 2025). Google Alerts has no API and fires on keywords, which misses the 'no protocol change, new meaning' notices. Broker FIX specs behind logins are out of reach for any web index, Exa included, and the pitch should say so.
exa_calls: Call 1, daily sweep (live, about 1 s, about $0.017). Endpoint: POST /search. Parameters: query 'Technical notice from an exchange, trade reporting facility, clearing agency or regulator announcing a change to FIX specifications, trading session hours, port or protocol migration, certification or testing dates, or a production go-live date'; type 'auto'; numResults 20 (10 above the base, at $1 per 1k each; kept under 25 because the Enterprise card lists requests above 25 results as an enterprise feature); includeDomains ['nasdaqtrader.com','cboe.com/notices','cboe.com/document/tech-spec','nyse.com','finra.org/filing-reporting/technical-notices','finra.org/rules-guidance/notices','dtcc.com','cmegroup.com/notices','sec.gov']; startPublishedDate '2026-09-01T00:00:00Z'; endPublishedDate = today; contents {highlights: {query: 'go-live or effective date, testing or certification dates, FIX tags or fields changed, action required', maxCharacters: 1000}}. Why: the domain list is the customer's own config, set in code and under version control, never chosen by a model. Path prefixes keep FINRA to its technical and regulatory notices. Highlights are steered to dates and actions because both the analyst and the next call read excerpts. Verified: a close variant of this filter set, run through Exa's keyless MCP, returned Nasdaq ETA 2026-39 and 2026-50, UTP 2026-29 and 2026-30, the Cboe EDGX expanded-hours notice, the NYSE extended-hours FAQ PDF and FINRA's ORF Native FIX reminder, all correctly dated.

Call 2, triage table (live, about 6 to 17 s, about $0.022). Endpoint: POST /search. Parameters: type 'deep'; the same domains, dates and query; additionalQueries ['23/5 overnight trading client testing schedule and production date', 'Native FIX port migration final cutover date', 'time in force or session changes for overnight trading', 'Treasury central clearing deadline for trading platform participants']; systemPrompt 'You triage market-structure and connectivity notices for a FIX onboarding team. One row per distinct change. If a later notice updates or withdraws an earlier one, report only the latest. Dates as YYYY-MM-DD, or not stated. Never infer a date.'; outputSchema {type:'object', required:['changes'], properties:{changes:{type:'array', items:{type:'object', required:[all six], properties:{venue, change, go_live_date, first_test_date, fix_impact (enum: new or changed FIX field, changed meaning of existing field, session hours, port or protocol migration, reporting rule, none stated), action_required}}}}}. That is 7 properties over 2 levels, inside the 10-property and 2-level limits, and the array defines its items. contents {highlights: true}. Why deep: a list of rows with 6 fields is exactly where the docs recommend deep types. output.grounding returns citations and a confidence for each cell path (for example changes[2].go_live_date), which the table shows as a link and a badge. The daily production job adds contents.maxAgeHours 24, because venue notices get updated in place (UTP 2026-30 is an 'UPDATE' notice). The live demo leaves it off to save latency.

Call 3, supersede check (live, about 1 s, $0.007). Endpoint: POST /search. Parameters: type 'auto'; numResults 5; query 'Is FINRA reducing the TRACE reporting timeframe from 15 minutes to one minute'; includeDomains ['finra.org','sec.gov']; startPublishedDate '2024-01-01T00:00:00Z'; contents {highlights: true}. Why: it shows why dated primary sources matter. The SEC approved one-minute TRACE reporting in Sep 2024, and FINRA's Regulatory Notice 25-17 (Dec 4, 2025) says FINRA is not moving forward with it. A team that built from the 2024 approval wasted the work. Verified in Exa's keyless MCP: 25-17 is the top hit, with the exact sentence as its highlight.

Call 4, production (shown as JSON, pre-run). Endpoint: POST /monitors. Parameters: name 'cutover-radar-us'; search {query: the Call 1 query, numResults 20, includeDomains: the same list, contents: {highlights: {query: the same, maxCharacters: 1000}}}; trigger {type:'interval', period:'1d'}; outputSchema: the Call 2 schema; metadata {team:'client-connectivity'}; webhook {url: the vendor's public HTTPS ticket bridge, events:['monitor.run.completed']}. Show one completed run fetched earlier with GET /monitors/{id}/runs/{runId}, and explain POST /monitors/{id}/trigger for on-demand runs. Why: $15 per 1k runs is about $0.015 a day. The webhookSecret is returned only once and must be stored. Runs can be up to 30 minutes late, which is fine for a daily sweep. The webhook cannot point at localhost, so the live demo does not depend on it.

Local step, no Exa call: the change rows are joined in pandas to an anonymized connectivity map (Clients A to E: routes, venues, FIX version, whether they report to TRF, ORF or TRACE, whether they trade overnight). Only public venue queries go to Exa and client names never leave the vendor, so unlike a holdings-driven workflow this one is safe without Zero Data Retention. Not used, on purpose: /answer, findSimilar, livecrawl, Websets. All calls go through the existing app/exa_client.py, which provides timeouts, 429 and 503 retries, requestId and cost logging, and the cached fallback.

proposed.business_impact: Assumptions to confirm in discovery: 15 connectivity analysts; about 3 hours a week each scanning notices today, cut to about 1 hour of reviewing the table; 50 working weeks; $100 an hour loaded cost; 3 missed-change incidents a year at about 60 staff-hours each. Time saved: 15 x 2 hours x 50 weeks = 1,500 hours a year, about $150K. Incidents: 3 x 60 = 180 hours, about $18K, before client credits and reputation, which the customer should price from its own incident log. Exa cost at list: the sweep is about $0.017, the deep triage about $0.022 and one Monitor run $0.015, so about $0.05 a day or under $20 a year, plus ad hoc questions at $0.007 each. The honest read for Exa: this internal use is cheap and sticky. proposed.problem:
US equities move to near 24-hour trading on Sun Dec 6, 2026. That is 65 days after the demo, and the demo day itself (Fri Oct 2) is test 1 of 6 on the industry calendar. The required changes are spread across at least six organizations in HTML alerts and PDFs. Verified examples:
- Nasdaq Equity Trader Alert 2026-46 (Aug 17): new order entry ports; open overnight orders cancelled at 4 AM; trades from 9 PM to midnight get the next trading day's trade date; a new halt code M1 for corporate actions; static LULD price bands (limit up/limit down, the rule that rejects orders priced too far from a reference price); a UAT (user acceptance testing) calendar starting Oct 2.
- Nasdaq ETA 2026-48 (Aug 20): separate overnight 9A/9B clearing relationships at NSCC, recommended by Oct 1. Without them, trades can be accepted at the trade reporting facility but rejected at NSCC.
- DTCC Important Notice A9689 (Jan 7): FIX tag 336 TradingSessionID with values PRE, REG, PST and OVN, conditionally required on trade input.
- DTCC note of May 28: TradeSuite ID accepts future-dated confirmations only from about 9:20 PM ET, after the nightly affirmation cutoff. Earlier submissions are rejected.
- NYSE Extended Hours FAQ v4.0 (Aug 2026): the NYSE Arca overnight session uses a new TradingSessionID value.
- Cboe EDGX has SEC approval for 23x5 trading in December.
- For fixed income, FINRA's Jul 31 notice sets the TRACE Native FIX cutover for Dec 11, 2026, and the SEC's Treasury cash-clearing deadline is Dec 31, 2026.

Today analysts read these notices one by one and map them to clients in spreadsheets. What goes wrong:
- A line buried in a PDF is missed, for example the trade-date roll. A buy-side allocation (FIX MsgType J) then carries TradeDate (tag 75) as the calendar date while the broker's confirm carries the next day, and the trade fails to match at DTCC CTM (the post-trade matching service).
- Or a broker is not ready, and the vendor learns about it from a client's rejected orders on launch night.

Email subscriptions exist for each venue and are the honest baseline. But they do not say which clients or brokers a change hits.

Google can find any single notice, but it cannot:

- return one row per notice with a citation and confidence for each field,

POST /search (main table). Body:
{query: 'Exchange, trade reporting facility and clearing notices announcing changes firms must make to order entry, FIX messages, trade reporting, clearing or confirmations for the overnight 23x5 trading session launching December 6, 2026',
type: 'deep',
numResults: 20,
includeDomains: ['nasdaqtrader.com','finra.org/filing-reporting/technical-notices','finra.org/rules-guidance/notices','dtcc.com','nyse.com/publicdocs','cboe.com/notices','cboe.com/us/equities/notices','cdn.cboe.com/resources','sec.gov/rules-regulations/self-regulatory-organization-rulemaking','sec.gov/files/rules/sro','federalregister.gov/documents','iextrading.com','memx.com'],
startPublishedDate: '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z',
additionalQueries: ['TradingSessionID tag 336 values for the overnight session','FINRA TRF 23/5 trade reporting specification and testing dates','NSCC overnight 9A/9B trading relationship requirement','future-dated confirmations and trade date for trades executed after 9 p.m. ET'],
systemPrompt: 'Prefer the venue or regulator notice over commentary. One row per distinct notice. Copy dates exactly as stated; leave a field empty rather than guess.',
contents: {highlights: {query: 'effective date, FIX tag, message type, testing date, action required'}},
outputSchema: {type:'object', required:['changes'], properties:{changes:{type:'array', items:{type:'object', required:['venue','notice_id','what_changes','action_required','affects'], properties:{venue, notice_id, effective_date, test_or_deadline_date, what_changes, action_required, affects (enum: order entry, trade reporting, clearing, confirmation/allocation, market data)}}}}}}

The schema has 8 properties, under the 10-property cap.

Why each choice:
- deep, because Exa's docs recommend deep types when outputSchema has several items and 3+ fields.
- The allowlist is loaded from venues.yaml in code, so the model can never widen or rewrite it. That is the same fix Ryan made in Pydantic AI.
- Path prefixes keep FINRA to its notice sections instead of all of finra.org.
- output.grounding gives every cell its own citations and a low/medium/high confidence.

Cost at list: $0.012 plus 10 extra results at $0.001 = $0.022 per run. Latency is 4 to 15 s plus about 2 s for synthesis, so the existing exa_client.py times out deep calls at 45 s and falls back to the cached run.

POST /contents (drill-down when the analyst clicks a row). Body:
{urls: [the row's cited URLs, e.g. 'https://www.dtcc.com/-/media/Files/pdf/2026/1/7/A9689.pdf'], highlights: {query: 'TradingSessionID tag 336 values and when it is required'}}

Why:
- It shows the exact passage (DTCC's PRE/REG/PST/OVN table) without reading the whole PDF.
- Options sit at the top level on /contents, with no contents wrapper.
- Raw HTTP avoids exa-py's silent 10,000-character text default, which would bill a second content type, and keeps the per-URL error tags in statuses visible.

Cost: $0.001 per page.

POST /monitors (how it runs in production; created before the call, triggered once live). Body:
{name: '23x5 readiness: venue and clearing notices', search: {query: <same as call 1>, numResults: 20, includeDomains: <same 13 entries>, contents: {highlights: true}}, trigger: {type: 'interval', period: '1d'}, outputSchema: <same schema>, metadata: {team: 'connectivity'}, webhook: {url: 'https://<vendor ticket bridge>/exa-hook', events: ['monitor.run.completed']}}
then POST /monitors/{id}/trigger.

Why:
- Monitors rerun the saved search on a schedule, deduplicate, and post output.content plus output.grounding to a webhook, so each new notice becomes a ticket that carries its citation.
- The webhook must be public HTTPS, not localhost.
- Runs can arrive up to 30 minutes late, which is fine for notices with weeks of lead time.

Cost: $0.015 per run, about $5.50 a year for one daily monitor.

proposed.name: Knowable at Trade Time: point-in-time evidence for trade surveillance alerts
proposed.one_liner: For a trade flagged just before a takeover announcement, pulls only what was public at the moment of the trade, pinned with Exa Snapshot and a published-date cutoff, and drafts a cited evidence record for the compliance case file.
proposed.customer:
A US asset manager (roughly $100B to $300B under management; a generic profile) whose compliance team reviews two alert streams:
- portfolio trades that its surveillance system flags as trading ahead of price-moving news;
- employees' personal trades, under the Code of Ethics review that SEC Rule 204A-1 requires of registered investment advisers.
Economic buyer: the Chief Compliance Officer with the compliance technology lead. The CISO runs security review (zero data retention, SOC 2 Type II). OEM alternative: a surveillance software vendor embeds this as an investigator feature and resells it to many firms.
proposed.problem:
Every alert needs a defensible answer to one question: what was public before this timestamp? Today the analyst searches a news terminal and Google with date tools and pastes links. Three things go wrong:
1. Hindsight leaks in. A story published after the trade ends up in the file, or a page is read as it looks today, after later edits.
2. The story that explains the trade often ran first in niche trade press, not on the wires.
3. Rationales vary by analyst and are hard to defend in an SEC or FINRA exam.

The real example used in the demo is MarineMax (NYSE: HZO):
- Donerail's $35-a-share offer became public in early February 2026 (Reuters, Feb 3).
- Reuters reported the sale process moving to a second round with a raised Donerail bid on May 7.
- On Jul 24, Reuters reported Blackstone and Donerail among the final bidders, and trade press repeated it Jul 25 to 28.
- On Mon Aug 10 a Reuters exclusive (carried by BNN Bloomberg) said Blackstone-owned Safe Harbor was nearing a deal, and the $53-a-share agreement was announced the same day.

In the demo, a fictional account buys HZO on Thu Aug 6 at 2:30 PM ET and gets flagged. A correct evidence record cites the July final-bidder reports and must not cite anything from Aug 10.
proposed.why_outside_web_content:
Bloomberg and Factiva are the timestamped system of record for wire news and should stay. Exa covers three gaps:
(a) The niche trade press where this story also ran: Superyacht Investor on Jul 25, Hedgeweek on Jul 27 (which also named Centerbridge), and Marine Industry News on Jul 28.
(b) Web pages that change after the fact. A published-date filter keeps later pages out, but it still shows today's text of the pages it keeps. Exa Snapshot returns the stored version of each page at or before the trade time, and omits pages Exa had no version of by then.
(c) An API that writes a cited, point-in-time record straight into the case system.

Competitors:
- Google has date tools in its UI, but its Custom Search JSON API is closed to new customers and ends Jan 1, 2027, and Gemini grounding does not let the developer set dates or domains (per Exa's comparison page).
- Bing's Search APIs were retired Aug 11, 2025.
- Perplexity's Search API has published-date and last-updated filters, and Tavily has start_date and end_date. Neither documents returning an earlier version of a page. Perplexity's last-updated filter would drop an edited page entirely rather than show what it said at the time.
- Zero data retention matters here because the query itself reveals which trade is under review. It is available for Exa Search and Contents, but not for Answer.

Sites checked on 2026-09-29:
- Through the keyless tier of Exa's hosted MCP server: the same query with endPublishedDate 2026-08-06 returned Reuters (Feb 3, Feb 25, May 7, Jul 24), marinebusiness.news (Feb 3), Superyacht Investor, Hedgeweek and Marine Industry News. With no cutoff, BNN Bloomberg's Aug 10 'nears deal' story ranked third and the Boating Industry deal story fifth.
- kelo.com: the syndicated text of the May 7 Reuters story.
- marineindustrynews.co.uk: the Feb 4 report of MarineMax's Feb 3 statement.
- Web search: the Aug 10 8-K on sec.gov, and Perplexity's and Tavily's docs on date filters.

- type auto, because Snapshot supports only auto, fast and instant.
- No category, because Snapshot rejects it.
- endPublishedDate keeps later pages out by date.
- snapshotAsOf goes inside contents on /search. It guarantees that every excerpt comes from the version Exa stored by the trade time.
- No maxAgeHours or livecrawlTimeout, because Snapshot rejects them.

proposed.name: Break Desk: primary-source evidence for corporate-action exceptions
proposed.one_liner: Sometimes an asset manager's security master disagrees with the market: a symbol change, a reverse split, a conditional bond call or an amended tender. Break Desk pulls the issuer's release, the SEC filing and the exchange alert, returns an evidence record with a citation on every field, and compares it field by field with the firm's own record before orders go out.
proposed.customer: A US asset manager with roughly $100B to $300B under management across equities and fixed income. It is not a former client of AJ, and no firm is named. Investment operations has about 60 people, including a reference data and corporate actions team of 8 to 10 analysts. That team owns the golden copy, meaning the firm's single cleaned security master. The buyer is the Head of Investment Operations (MD level), who owns the data-vendor budget. The Chief Data Officer and information security must approve any outside service whose queries reveal holdings.
proposed.end_user: A reference data and corporate actions analyst. The day starts around 7 AM with an exception queue fed by the security master, the OMS (order management system) and the custodian reconciliation. Typical items are orders rejected for an unknown symbol, positions that no longer match the custodian, bonds flagged as called, and two data vendors that disagree. For each unexplained item the analyst searches the web and reads issuer releases, 8-Ks and exchange alerts. Then they decide who is wrong (the vendor, the custodian or the firm's own mapping), fix the golden copy or escalate to the vendor, and write a note for the audit file. The US has settled on T+1 since May 28, 2024, so allocations and affirmations are expected on trade date and the queue has to be cleared early.
proposed.problem:
The decision is: what actually happened to this security, when did it happen, and is our record right? Today each exception needs a manual research session, assumed at 20 to 30 minutes. A wrong fix turns into rejected orders, position breaks, bad NAV prices or settlement fails. Real September 2026 cases show what goes wrong:
(1) FG Nexus renamed itself FG Communities Holdings. The issuer's GlobeNewswire release (Sep 24) says FGNX becomes FGC and FGNXP becomes FGCPP at the open on Mon Sep 28. A MarketScreener item dated Sep 27 reports the change backwards ("to FGNX from FGC"). The same issuer also did a 1-for-5 reverse split with a new CUSIP in Feb 2026 (Nasdaq ECA 2026-91), so its identifiers have changed twice this year.
(2) OpenText's tender offer for its 3.875% notes due 2028 changed after launch. The Sep 23 release said up to $450M, expiring Sep 29. An amendment on Sep 25 cut the cap to $300M and moved expiration to Sep 30, 5 PM New York time. A record loaded on the 23rd was wrong by the 25th.
(3) OpenText's $1.0B 6.900% senior secured notes due 2027 have a conditional full redemption on Oct 2, 2026, the demo day. It depends on proceeds from the new 6.700% 2031 and 7.150% 2033 notes, which priced Sep 23 with closing expected Oct 1. A vendor that marks the bond as called before the condition is met can be wrong.
(4) Nauticus Robotics (KITT) did a 1-for-6 reverse split effective Sep 25 with new CUSIP 63911H504 (Nasdaq ECA 2026-671, published Sep 23). Custodian and OMS quantities disagree until the split is booked.
proposed.why_outside_web_content:
Licensed feeds (Bloomberg, LSEG/Refinitiv, ICE and DTCC's corporate-actions data) are the system of record and stay that way. Exa is the tiebreaker and evidence layer, not a replacement.

The exception queue exists because those feeds arrive late, disagree with each other or with the custodian, or miss a change made mid-event. The tiebreaker is always the primary document: the issuer release, the 8-K or the exchange alert. A terminal shows the vendor's normalized record, not a dated primary-source link that can be attached to the ticket and the audit file.

Google can find the page when an analyst searches by hand. But ranking mixes in aggregators (the reversed FG Nexus item above). It cannot be locked in code to primary domains and a date window that stops at the exception date. It returns links rather than fields that can be compared. The research file also says Google's programmatic search API is closing to new customers; re-check that before saying it.

Confidentiality matters too: an asset manager's search queries reveal what it holds. Exa offers zero data retention (ZDR) for Search and Contents on Enterprise plans.

Public content I checked on 2026-09-29:
- globenewswire.com: FG Nexus release, Sep 24
- marketscreener.com: the reversed Sep 27 headline
- nasdaqtrader.com: ECA 2026-671 (KITT) and ECA 2026-91 (FGNX split); search results also listed Safe Harbor, VerifyMe and Matinas reverse splits with new CUSIPs
- sec.gov, OpenText 8-K exhibits: Sep 22 conditional redemption, Sep 23 pricing, Sep 23 tender, Sep 25 amendment
- ir.truist.com: Sep 17 redemption of $850M subordinated notes due Oct 30, 2026 on Sep 30, CUSIP 07330MAA5 (a backup bond example)
exa_calls:
1. Discovery, while the analyst waits. POST /search with:
  - query: 'FG Nexus Inc. ticker symbol and name change effective September 28, 2026'
  - type: 'auto'
  - numResults: 10
  - includeDomains: ['globenewswire.com', 'businesswire.com', 'prnewswire.com', 'accessnewswire.com', 'sec.gov', 'nasdaqtrader.com', 'nyse.com', 'dtcc.com'], plus the issuer website from the security master record, for example 'fgnexus.io', added by code
  - startPublishedDate: '2026-09-14T00:00:00Z' (exception date minus 14 days)
  - endPublishedDate: '2026-09-28T23:59:59Z' (the exception date, so nothing published later can leak in)
  - contents: {highlights: {query: 'old symbol, new symbol, effective date, new CUSIP, split ratio', maxCharacters: 800}}
Why: auto is the default type, about 1 s at $7 per 1,000, with contents for the first 10 results included. The domain list is set in code, so neither the analyst nor a model can widen it to aggregators. The date window keeps the evidence point-in-time. Highlights steered by a query return the passage that matters, not whole pages.

2. Contrast, clicked once. The same /search with includeDomains removed. Why: it shows what the open web returns, including secondary sites. That is the reason the allowlist lives in code rather than in the query.

3. Evidence record. POST /search with:
  - query: 'Corporate action affecting FG Nexus Inc. (Nasdaq: FGNX) on September 28, 2026: event type, old and new symbols, effective date, CUSIP, status'
  - type: 'deep'
  - additionalQueries: ['FG Communities Holdings FGC FGCPP symbol change', 'Nasdaq corporate actions alert FG Nexus']
  - includeDomains, startPublishedDate and endPublishedDate: the same as call 1
  - systemPrompt: 'Use only issuer releases, SEC filings and exchange notices. When terms were amended, prefer the most recent document. If sources disagree, describe the disagreement in conflicts. Leave a field empty rather than infer it.'
  - outputSchema: {type: 'object', required: ['event_type', 'issuer', 'effective_date', 'status'], properties: {event_type, issuer, effective_date (YYYY-MM-DD), old_identifier, new_identifier, new_cusip, terms, status (described as announced, conditional, amended, effective or withdrawn), conflicts}}. That is 9 string properties, under the 10-property cap, with no nesting.
  - contents: {highlights: true}
Why: deep is Exa's recommended type when a schema asks for three or more fields. It returns output.content plus output.grounding, which gives each field its citations and a low, medium or high confidence, so every value on the card links to its source. The schema has no citation fields because grounding supplies them. Deep takes 4 to 15 s plus about 2 s of synthesis and costs $12 per 1,000.

4. Fresh re-check for events still in motion (the conditional call, the amended tender). The same deep call with contents: {highlights: true, maxAgeHours: 24}. Why: maxAgeHours 24 makes Exa re-fetch any page it cached more than a day ago, so an amendment or an Oct 1 closing notice is not read from a stale copy. It controls how fresh the returned page text is, not which pages exist. It is used only here because it adds latency.

5. Audit copy. POST /contents with:
  - urls: [<issuer release URL>, <exchange alert URL>]
  - snapshotAsOf: '2026-09-25T20:00:00Z'
  - highlights: {query: 'symbol, effective date'}
Why: Exa Snapshot (launched Sep 17, 2026) returns the page as Exa stored it at trade-date close, so the ticket records what was knowable then. On /contents the options sit at the top level. A per-URL CONTENT_NOT_CACHED status is shown without failing the call. snapshotAsOf cannot be combined with maxAgeHours. Pay-as-you-go covers a rolling 5-month window and 100 requests before a sales conversation, and the POC plan budgets for that.

6. Deliberately not used, and plumbing:
  - /answer: it does not support ZDR, and this buyer needs ZDR because queries reveal holdings.
  - findSimilar: deprecated.
  - Agent API: asynchronous. It is reserved for a later overnight backfill at a fixed low effort ($0.025 per run), shown only from a cached run.
  - Every response logs requestId, searchTime and costDollars.
  - 429 and 503 responses retry and honor Retry-After (a 503 is not billed).
  - The UI waits 20 seconds, then falls back to the saved run (existing exa_client.py cache).

  - Slide 3: the architecture. Exception queue, then Exa Search (primary-domain allowlist and date window set in code), then an evidence record with per-field citations, then the field comparison, then the escalation. Add ZDR and SOC 2 Type II as the enterprise requirements.

Close, 5 minutes: the business-impact arithmetic, the POC plan and success criteria, then two discovery questions for the room.
proposed.business_impact:
The value is analyst hours given back, measured as time per exception. All numbers below are assumptions to confirm in discovery.

Assumptions:
- 30 exceptions a day need outside evidence
- 25 minutes each today
- 250 trading days a year
- $110 an hour fully loaded

Today: 30 x 25 min = 12.5 h/day, so 3,125 h/yr, or about $344K.

With Break Desk, the analyst reads the card, clicks the citation and approves: about 8 min each. That is 4 h/day, 1,000 h/yr, about $110K.

Savings: about 2,125 h, roughly $234K a year, or about one analyst's research time returned.

Floor case: 10 exceptions a day with 10 minutes saved each is still about 417 h, or roughly $46K a year.

Exa cost per exception at list prices: one auto search ($0.007) + one deep search ($0.012) + two Snapshot pages ($0.002), about $0.02. Across 7,500 exceptions a year that is about $160. Even 10x for re-checks stays under $2K.

Not counted, but real: fewer wrong fixes, meaning fewer rejected orders, position breaks and settlement fails under T+1.

POC, 2 weeks:
- Eval set: 150 closed exception tickets from the last 60 days with known resolutions. Each is re-run with endPublishedDate set to the time the ticket opened, so there is no hindsight.
- Success criteria:
  - event type, effective date and new identifier match the final resolution on at least 90% of tickets
  - a primary-source citation on at least 95%
  - median time to evidence under 20 s
  - in a one-week shadow on live exceptions, analyst handling time down at least 50%
- Credits: under $25.
- Production needs an Enterprise plan for ZDR, which gives the AE (account executive) a natural commercial path.

Expansion: onboarding backfills (checking a new fund's full holdings for pending events) through the Agent API, then fixed-income new-issue setup.

proposed.name: Change Radar: venue and clearing notices to test-ready tickets for the 23x5 go-live
proposed.one_liner: For a trading-technology vendor, Change Radar watches exchange, FINRA and DTCC technical notices and turns each one into a cited change ticket: effective date, test windows, FIX tags and feed fields touched, and action required. It lays the tickets on a readiness calendar ahead of the Dec 6 to 7, 2026 move to 23-hour trading.
proposed.customer: A trading-technology vendor, such as an OMS/EMS provider or a FIX connectivity network, serving about 150 buy-side and sell-side client firms. No former employer or client is named. It has a client connectivity and onboarding team of 20 to 30 plus a market-structure product group. The buyer is the Head of Client Connectivity or the COO (MD level), who owns release risk and client SLAs (service-level agreements). The same pattern fits a broker-dealer's electronic trading technology group.
proposed.end_user:
A market-structure and connectivity analyst.
- Reads trader alerts, technical notices, specification PDFs and rule filings from a few dozen venues and infrastructure providers.
- Decides which ones touch the product's venue adapters, FIX sessions, market-data handlers, and trade-date and settlement logic.
- Opens Jira tickets with effective dates and test windows.
- Tells client services which clients are affected.
- Books UAT (user acceptance testing) and certification slots.
This autumn the job is much heavier, because every US equity venue and market utility is changing for extended hours at the same time.
proposed.problem:
The decision is: which market-structure changes hit our product, by when, and what must we test before the last weekend UAT? These changes are on the public web now:
- Nasdaq Equity Trader Alert (ETA) 2026-46: a new 9 PM to 4 AM ET session from Dec 6, 2026. It needs new order entry ports. Trades between 9 PM and midnight get the next trading day's trade date. Weekend UATs are Oct 2, 16 and 30, Nov 6 and 20, and Dec 4.
- Cboe notice 60737: Cboe One feed timestamps switch from nanoseconds since midnight to nanoseconds since epoch on Nov 2, 2026, ahead of EDGX moving to 23x5 on trade date Dec 7. A certification feed has been available since Aug 31.
- DTCC's UTC 24x5 one-pager: a new FIX tag 715 (ClearingBusinessDate) on UTC real-time output, and FIX tag 336 (TradingSessionID) required for firms sending overnight trades. NSCC clearing has run 24x5 since June 29, 2026.
- FINRA technical notice, Aug 14, 2026: the trade reporting facilities (TRFs) move to 23x5 on Dec 6 with a nightly 8 PM pause, and overnight clearing relationships must be set up separately.
- Nasdaq ETA 2026-39 and 2026-55: TRF FIX and trade-journal spec updates, and TRF software changes on Nov 2.
- NYSE lists overnight, early, core and late sessions, with launch 'targeted' for 2026.
The costs today are analyst hours spent reading, triaging and comparing spec versions. The big cost is a change caught after the final UAT on Dec 4. That becomes an out-of-cycle release or a client-facing defect on go-live night, for example a feed handler that still assumes midnight-based timestamps, or allocations stamped with the wrong trade date under T+1.
proposed.why_outside_web_content:
Licensed data (Bloomberg, LSEG) carries prices and reference data. It does not carry venue technical notices, test calendars or spec revision tables. Venue email lists exist, but they are per venue, unstructured and not tied to a change log.

Google finds a notice if you already know to look. It cannot be locked in code to a venue domain list and a date window, and it returns links, not dated fields.

proposed.name: Break Check: primary-source evidence for corporate-action exceptions
proposed.one_liner: When two licensed data feeds disagree about a split, ticker or CUSIP change, the ops analyst gets the issuer's own release and the listing exchange's notice side by side in about 4 seconds. Every field is cited, and code flags the disagreement, not a model.
proposed.customer: A US asset manager with roughly $100B to $200B under management (a size chosen for the example). It runs an order management system fed by a vendor-sourced security master, meaning the firm's golden record of every instrument: identifiers, share terms and corporate actions. Investment operations has a 6 to 10 person security master and corporate actions team that clears a daily exception queue whenever its two licensed feeds disagree. Fund administrators and middle-office outsourcers have the same need at larger scale. Buyer: the head of investment operations or data governance. Technical owner: the ops engineering or data platform lead. This is a customer type, not a former client of AJ.
proposed.end_user: Security master and corporate actions analyst. The day starts around 7 AM with an exception queue built from overnight vendor loads: two feeds disagree on a split ratio, an effective date, a new CUSIP (the 9-character US security identifier) or a ticker. Every break has to be cleared before the trading desk starts and before the NAV (net asset value) cut-off. For each one the analyst opens the issuer's press release, the exchange's corporate-action alert and sometimes an 8-K, decides which source is right, loads the fix, pastes the evidence into the ticket and escalates to the data vendor if the vendor was wrong.
proposed.problem: The decision is which value to load (ratio, effective date, new CUSIP or ticker) and on which day. Today that takes manual research, roughly 15 minutes per break (an assumption to confirm), with the evidence pasted in by hand. What goes wrong is that dates really are ambiguous. A real example from this week: CDT Equity's own release (GlobeNewswire, Sept 25, 2026) says its 1-for-25 reverse split becomes effective September 28, 2026 at 5:00 PM ET, with split-adjusted trading from the open on September 29. Nasdaq's Equity Corporate Actions Alert #2026-683 gives the effective date as Tuesday, September 29. Same ratio, same new CUSIP 20678X700, but 'effective date' means something different in each. Suppose a feed loads the split for September 28. That day's positions are then split-adjusted against an unadjusted closing price, so the position can be misvalued by the full factor of 25 in that day's NAV and risk reports. A stale CUSIP after the change makes trades and allocations fail to match downstream: the 'busted trades' AJ worked at Charles River. The web also changes under you. On Sept 29, Exa's cached copy of Nasdaq alert #2026-677 (Cheetah Net, 1-for-150) read 'Page Not Available' while the live page had the full alert.
proposed.why_outside_web_content:
Licensed data does not settle it on its own. Bloomberg, LSEG (Refinitiv), ICE and DTCC offer corporate-action data services, and they stay the system of record. But the exception only exists because those feeds disagree, lag or record an ambiguous date, and a feed cannot be evidence against itself. The tie-breaker is the primary source: the issuer's release on a newswire, the listing exchange's alert, or the SEC filing. Those are public web pages, not fields in a licensed feed.

Google does not fit the workflow either. A human can find the release with Google, but not as an automated step inside the exception queue. Google offers no single call that combines a domain allowlist set in code, a published-date window and per-field extraction with citations. Its Custom Search JSON API is closed to new customers and ends Jan 1, 2027.

Privacy is a third reason. The query itself reveals holdings (issuer and CUSIP), so it needs a provider with zero data retention (ZDR, meaning the provider stores nothing). Exa offers ZDR on Enterprise for Search and Contents, and those are the only two endpoints this design uses. It deliberately avoids /answer, which ZDR does not cover.

1. Issuer-side evidence (live, run in parallel with call 2).
- Request: POST /search {query: 'CDT Equity (Nasdaq: CDT) press release announcing a reverse stock split: split ratio, effective date and time, first split-adjusted trading day, new CUSIP', type: 'auto', numResults: 5, includeDomains: ['globenewswire.com','prnewswire.com','businesswire.com','accessnewswire.com','nasdaq.com/press-release','finance.yahoo.com','sec.gov'], startPublishedDate: '2026-09-01T00:00:00Z' (about 30 days before the break), contents: {highlights: {query: 'split ratio, effective date and time, split-adjusted trading, new CUSIP'}}, systemPrompt: 'Use only the announcement or SEC filing from the company with ticker CDT. Ignore other companies. Copy dates exactly as the source writes them. Write not stated for any field the source does not give. If two sources of this type disagree, give both values with their dates.', outputSchema: {type: 'object', required: [all 7], properties: {ticker, event_type ('reverse split, forward split, ticker change, name change, ADS ratio change, or other'), ratio, effective ('date and time exactly as stated'), first_trading_day_new_terms ('YYYY-MM-DD'), new_cusip, new_symbols}, all strings}}.
- Why auto, not deep: the domain list and date window already point at the right pages, so query expansion would add cost ($12 vs $7 per 1,000) and latency without adding sources.
- Why highlights: a model reads them.
- Why domains in code: neither the user nor a model can widen them.
- Why this outputSchema: 7 properties is under the 10-property cap, and I add no citation fields of my own. It returns output.content plus output.grounding, so every field carries its source URL and a low/medium/high confidence.
- Why the mirror domains: Business Wire's own copy of the VerifyMe release did not come back in my check, but its Yahoo Finance syndication did.
- Expected: the GlobeNewswire release of Sept 25 with 1-for-25, effective Sept 28 at 5:00 PM ET, trading adjusted from Sept 29, CUSIP 20678X700.
- Measured through the keyless MCP, without outputSchema: 1.35 s, with the release ranked first. The docs say outputSchema adds about 2 s.

2. Exchange-side evidence (live, in parallel with call 1).
- Request: POST /search with the same systemPrompt and outputSchema, query: 'Nasdaq Equity Corporate Actions Alert for CDT Equity Inc. (CDT) reverse stock split and CUSIP number change', type: 'auto', numResults: 5, includeDomains: ['nasdaqtrader.com'], startPublishedDate: '2026-09-01T00:00:00Z', contents: {highlights: {query: 'effective date, split ratio, new CUSIP'}}.
- Why a separate call: in my check, a single mixed-domain query ranked the CDT release first but returned other issuers' Nasdaq alerts (#2026-651 and 654) instead of CDT's #683. With one call per source type, the grounding for these fields can only point at the exchange, so the comparison is source against source by design.
- What the code does next:
  - keeps only results whose text contains the ticker or CUSIP
  - compares the two records field by field with fixed rules
  - flags any grounding citation outside that call's allowed domains
- Expected: alert #2026-683, 1-25, effective Tuesday Sept 29, 2026, CUSIP 20678X700.
- Measured analog: 2.6 s for a 10-result nasdaqtrader.com query.

3. Stale-page repair (live, only when triggered).
- Trigger: an exchange result's highlight contains 'Page Not Available', or its fields come back 'not stated'.
- Request: POST /contents {urls: ['https://www.nasdaqtrader.com/TraderNews.aspx?id=ECA2026-677'], maxAgeHours: 0, livecrawlTimeout: 12000, highlights: {query: 'effective date, split ratio, new CUSIP'}}. On /contents these options sit at the top level, not inside contents.
- Why: maxAgeHours 0 forces a live fetch of that one page, instead of paying live-crawl latency on every search result. The 12,000 ms timeout follows the docs' advice for slow sites.
- If the crawl fails: statuses[] shows it (CRAWL_TIMEOUT, CRAWL_LIVECRAWL_TIMEOUT). The app then keeps the stale copy, flags it and escalates.
- Verified Sept 29: with the default cache, a search returned 'Page Not Available' for this alert in 1.6 s. The same search with maxAgeHours 0 and livecrawlTimeout 12000 returned the real alert (1-for-150, effective Monday Sept 28) in 3.1 s.
- Cost: $1 per 1,000 pages.

4. Audit trail (optional, pre-run and cached, never live).
- Request: POST /contents {urls: [the CDT release URL, the Nasdaq #2026-683 URL], snapshotAsOf: '2026-09-28T13:00:00Z', highlights: true}.
- Shows what each source said at 9 AM ET on the day the exception was worked. That answers the auditor's question 'what did we know when we loaded it'. It is the same point-in-time discipline AJ enforced in his paper-trading research system.
- Why not live: Snapshot is a research preview:
  - rolling 5-month window on pay-as-you-go
  - 100 requests before a sales conversation
  - no deep types and no category
  - cannot be combined with maxAgeHours
  - returns CONTENT_NOT_CACHED if Exa stored no copy at that time
- If the pre-run returns CONTENT_NOT_CACHED, drop this panel.

5. Pre-flight check already done (not part of the app).
- On Sept 29 I made 21 calls through Exa's keyless hosted MCP (https://mcp.exa.ai/mcp, tool web_search_advanced_exa). That tool passes type, includeDomains, startPublishedDate, highlights and maxAgeHours through to search.
- Latency, including the MCP hop: median about 2.8 s, 14 of 21 under 4 s, and three outliers at 8.2, 12.9 and 14.6 s.
- The keyless tool cannot send outputSchema or deep types, so calls 1 and 2 with outputSchema stay untested until AJ has a key.
- AJ can rerun the same probes before signing up.

proposed.name: Venue Change Radar: exchange technical notices triaged into dated action items
proposed.one_liner: Four parallel Exa searches read the last three weeks of exchange, FINRA and OCC technical notices and return one cited row per notice: what changes, by when, and whether it is mandatory. Code then joins those rows to the firm's own FIX sessions, so the connectivity team sees which sessions break and by what date.
proposed.customer: A mid-size US broker-dealer or execution-services firm that is a direct member of about a dozen equity and options exchanges and reports trades to the FINRA TRFs (trade reporting facilities). Its electronic trading connectivity team has 6 to 8 people. Trading-technology vendors that run exchange gateways for many brokers have the same need. Buyer: the head of electronic trading technology. Technical owner: the connectivity or trading-systems lead. This is a customer type, not a former client of AJ.
proposed.end_user:
Exchange connectivity or trading systems analyst. A typical day:
- watches FIX sessions at the open
- onboards clients to DMA and algos
- books weekend certification tests
- keeps disaster-recovery (DR) runbooks current
- reads the email notices each venue sends: Nasdaq Trader alerts, MIAX alerts, Cboe notices, FINRA technical notices, OCC info memos and SIP plan alerts (the SIP is the consolidated market data tape)

For each notice the analyst decides whether it needs a spec change, a config change, a test slot or nothing, and opens tickets. This quarter that includes the move to 23-hour trading.
proposed.problem:
The weekly decision is which venue changes need action from us, by when, and for which sessions. Today a senior analyst reads every notice by hand across 10 or more mailing lists and forwards the ones that matter. The real cost is a miss, which only shows up when a session fails.

Real examples on the web right now:
- Nasdaq Options Technical Update #2026-9 (dated Aug 4) moves disaster-recovery FIX port IP addresses. The new addresses are required from Monday Nov 2 for PHLX, NTX Options and NOM, and from Monday Dec 14 for ISE, GEMX and MRX. A firm that misses it finds out on the day it fails over.
- MIAX Futures' alert of Sept 28 makes FIX Drop, Depth of Market and Top of Market v1.3 mandatory on Sunday Nov 8.
- The FINRA/Nasdaq TRFs move to 23/5 hours (9 PM ET Sunday to 8 PM ET Friday) on Dec 6, 2026, per Nasdaq ETA #2026-39 and FINRA's technical notice of July 10. Industry weekend UAT (user acceptance testing) runs on Oct 2, 16 and 30, Nov 6 and 20, with a confidence test on Dec 4 (Nasdaq ETA #2026-50 and UTP Vendor Alert #2026-30).

The first of those UAT weekends starts at 11 PM ET on Friday Oct 2, a few hours after this interview.
proposed.why_outside_web_content:
Licensed data does not cover it. Bloomberg and LSEG sell prices and reference data; they do not deliver the venues' technical notices as data. Each venue publishes on its own site and email list, in its own format:
- Nasdaq Trader alert series ETA, ETU, OTU, UTP and DN
- MIAX alerts
- Cboe notices
- FINRA technical notices
- OCC info memos
So firms subscribe to each list and triage by hand.

Google does not fit either. It finds a notice once you know it exists, but it cannot run a daily query across a code-set list of a dozen venue domains, within a date window, and return one structured, cited row per notice. Its Custom Search JSON API is also closed to new customers and ends Jan 1, 2027.

Content check on Sept 29 through Exa's keyless hosted MCP:
- Indexed with dates: Nasdaq Trader alerts, MIAX alerts, FINRA technical notices, OCC info memos and the UTP plan's data feed spec.
- Partial: Cboe returned some notices plus index pages.
- Weak: NYSE returned rule filings, an extended-hours FAQ PDF and the trader-update index page, but no individual trader updates.

I cross-checked Nasdaq OTU #2026-9, ETA #2026-39 and the MIAX Onyx alert with WebFetch.
exa_calls:
1. Scan (live): four POST /search calls in parallel, one per venue group, so Nasdaq's volume cannot crowd out smaller venues.
- Shared parameters: query 'technical notice telling member firms about a change to order entry, drop copy, trade reporting, connectivity or IP addresses, trading hours, or required testing, with an effective date', type: 'auto', numResults: 10, startPublishedDate: '2026-09-11T00:00:00Z' (21 days back), contents: {highlights: {query: 'what member firms must do and by when: effective date, mandatory or optional, testing dates, specification version, IP addresses'}}.
- includeDomains per group:
  - ['nasdaqtrader.com']
  - ['miaxglobal.com']
  - ['cboe.com']
  - ['finra.org','infomemo.theocc.com','utpplan.com','ctaplan.com','24exchange.com','txse.com','iextrading.com','memx.com']
- Why: auto at $7 per 1,000 is enough because the domains already define the set of pages. Highlights because a model reads the output next. Four calls stay under the 10 requests per second limit.
- Measured analogs through the keyless MCP: 1.1 to 2.4 s for nasdaqtrader.com, 1.8 s for finra.org, 3.6 s for the MIAX-and-others group, 8.2 s for cboe.com.

2. Triage: the same four calls also carry outputSchema and systemPrompt.
- outputSchema: {type: 'object', required: ['notices'], properties: {notices: {type: 'array', items: {type: 'object', properties: {title, notice_date ('date printed on the notice, YYYY-MM-DD'), effective_date ('first date the change applies, YYYY-MM-DD, or none'), action ('one of: spec change, connectivity or IP change, testing or certification, hours change, fee or rule only, no member action'), mandatory ('yes, no, or not stated'), systems ('interfaces named, such as FIX order entry, FIX Drop, TRF FIX, DR ports'), what_to_do ('one sentence')}}}}}. That is 8 properties with one array that has items, under the 10-property cap.
- systemPrompt: 'One row per notice page in the results. Use the date printed on the notice, not the crawl date. If the notice says no member action is required, say so. Do not merge notices or invent dates.'
- Why: output.grounding gives each cell (for example notices[2].effective_date) its source URL and a confidence, so any row the analyst acts on is one click from the venue's own page. notice_date is extracted separately because Exa's publishedDate is an estimate: OTU #2026-9 is dated Aug 4 on the page, but Exa had Aug 31.
- What the code does next:
  - sorts by effective_date
  - flags mandatory items due within 45 days
  - collapses fee-only and no-action rows
  - checks that every citation is on that group's domains
- Fallback if auto returns thin rows: type 'deep-lite' (about 4 s, $12 per 1,000; its 5 requests per second limit is still fine for 4 calls).

3. Drill-down (live, one click on a row).
- Request: POST /contents {urls: ['https://www.nasdaqtrader.com/TraderNews.aspx?id=OTU2026-9'], text: {maxCharacters: 6000}, maxAgeHours: 24, livecrawlTimeout: 12000}. On /contents these options sit at the top level.
- Why full text: here a human reads the whole notice, including its IP and port table. That is the case where full text is right, unlike the model-facing calls.
- Why maxAgeHours 24: it re-fetches if Exa's copy is more than a day old. Venues edit notices in place and publish UPDATE versions; UTP #2026-30 is an update of #2026-29.
- Cost: $1 per 1,000 pages.

4. Production path (shown on a slide, not live): one POST /monitors per venue group.
- Request: {name: 'Nasdaq technical notices', search: {query: same as call 1, numResults: 10, includeDomains: ['nasdaqtrader.com'], contents: {highlights: true}}, trigger: {type: 'interval', period: '1d'}, outputSchema: the triage schema, webhook: {url: 'https://<customer ticketing bridge>/exa', events: ['monitor.run.completed']}}.
- Why: scheduled runs post new notices straight into the customer's ticketing system.
- Why not live: the webhook must be public HTTPS, not localhost, so it cannot run inside a local Streamlit demo.
- Runs can be up to 30 minutes late, which is fine for a daily sweep. Price: $15 per 1,000 runs.
- In a POC, POST /monitors/{id}/trigger forces a run on demand.

5. Pre-flight check already done (not part of the app).
- The Sept 29 keyless MCP probes included four single-venue probes and one multi-venue probe for this idea. They returned:
  - Nasdaq ETA #2026-38, 50, 51, 53 and 54
  - UTP #2026-29 and 30, DN #2026-8 and OTU #2026-9
  - MIAX Onyx, Pearl and Sapphire alerts
  - FINRA's TRF extended-hours technical notice and an OCC info memo on Extended Trading Hours
- outputSchema stays untested until AJ has a key.
demo_flow:
Slides 1 and 2 (about 5 minutes):
- Who: a connectivity analyst at a broker-dealer that is a member of about 12 venues.
- The decision: which venue changes need action from us, and by when.
- The forcing event: TRF 23/5 hours on Dec 6, with the first industry weekend UAT starting tonight at 11 PM ET.
- The cost of a miss: a DR port that will not log in on the day you fail over.
- Thesis: Exa turns a dozen mailing lists into one cited, dated change log, joined to our own sessions.

Screen 1, Scan: set the window to 21 days. Before clicking Scan, say the hypothesis: 'Four searches in parallel, one per venue group. Domains are fixed in code, the type is auto, and highlights are aimed at what members must do and by when. If Exa is doing its job, Nasdaq's TRF 23/5 testing alert and the MIAX Onyx mandatory upgrade show up with their own sentences within about 4 seconds.' Click Scan. Show each call's latency, cost and request JSON.

Screen 2, Change log: one row per notice, sorted by effective date.
- Red: mandatory within 45 days (MIAX FIX Drop v1.3 on Nov 8).
- Amber: testing windows (UAT from Oct 2 to Dec 4).
- Grey: no member action (the MIAX Pearl Equities technology refresh says members need no changes).
Hover a cell to see its grounding citation and confidence, and click one to open the venue's page live.

Screen 3, What breaks for us: the app joins the rows to a mocked connectivity inventory CSV (session name, venue, protocol, DR yes or no, clients enabled for overnight trading). Example output: 'ISE, GEMX, MRX DR order-entry sessions: 3 must switch IP by Dec 14' and 'TRF FIX sessions: 2 need a UAT slot before Dec 4'. Say plainly that the inventory is mocked and the notices are live. Export tickets as CSV with source links.

Drill-down: widen the window to 60 days and click the OTU #2026-9 row. /contents returns full text with the IP and port table, because a human is reading it. Point out that Exa dated this notice Aug 31 while the page says Aug 4, which is why the schema extracts notice_date.

Unexpected query: ask Ryan to name a venue. Type its domain into the free-form group (for example iextrading.com) and rerun just that call. If coverage is thin, as NYSE was in my check, say so and show the POC plan: measure per-venue coverage, then use /contents on known notice pages or an Enterprise custom index.

Failure drill: toggle 'simulate timeout' on one of the four calls. Three groups render live and the fourth shows its cached run with the saved-at time. Say: 'Partial results beat a spinner, and the requestId is logged.'

Slide 3 (about 5 minutes):
- Production: four daily Monitors posting to their ticketing webhook.
- Business-impact arithmetic.
- A 3-week POC that replays the last 90 days against the team's own ticket history. Success criteria:
  - recall of at least 95% of the notices they actually acted on
  - precision of at least 90% on the mandatory flag
  - publication-to-index lag under 24 hours, measured with daily Monitors
  - a per-venue coverage table
- Optional Snapshot replay inside its 5-month window, with the caveat that Snapshot fixes page content at the cutoff date but not ranking.
proposed.business_impact:
The head of electronic trading technology measures this in missed or late venue changes (incidents and failed certifications), and in analyst hours.

Volume from the web: by late September, Nasdaq alone had issued about 105 numbered technical alerts in 2026 (ETA #55, UTP #30, OTU #9, DN #8, ETU #3), about 12 a month. Assuming 5 or 6 venue families of similar volume gives about 60 to 80 notices a month, or 15 to 20 a week (assumption).

Hours saved:
- Today: 18 notices x 6 minutes = about 1.8 hours a week for a senior analyst to read and route, about 95 hours a year, or about $9.5K at $100 an hour loaded.
- With the radar, review drops to about 30 minutes a week, saving about 70 hours ($7K).

That saving is small, and I would say so. The case rests on misses. Value = $7K + (incidents avoided x cost per incident). Assume one avoided client-impacting incident a year (a DR failover that fails, or sessions rejected after a mandatory upgrade) at about 80 staff hours ($8K) plus SLA credits. That puts the value at $15K or more a year, before counting a missed 23/5 certification slot that delays overnight trading for clients. The deciding number is the team's own count of venue changes they caught late last year, which is discovery question one.

Exa cost:
- 4 searches a day at $7 per 1,000 = $0.028 a day, about $7 a year.
- As four daily Monitors: 1,460 runs x $0.015 = about $22 a year.

What Exa gets out of it is breadth. A trading-technology vendor can embed the same feed for every broker it serves, and the pattern extends to broker algo notices, market-data vendor changes and regulator releases.

# Break Check: build and demo spec

Demo: Fri 2026-10-02, 6:30 PM ET, Exa FDE demo round with Ryan Ahern. 30 minutes.

Nothing in this spec has been run with an API key yet. Every expected result below comes from the Sep 29 research: keyless MCP probes plus WebFetch checks on primary pages. Re-verify each row on its primary page on Wednesday before saying it out loud.

---

## 1. The customer, the end user, and the problem

1. **The customer.** A mid-size US asset manager (assume $100B to $200B under management, equities plus investment-grade bonds) buys security data from two licensed vendors and merges it into one "golden copy". The golden copy is the master record of every instrument its order system trades. The buyer is the Head of Investment Operations, who owns the data-vendor budget.
2. **The end user.** The security master analyst starts around 7 AM on a queue of "breaks". A break is a row where the two vendors disagree about something: a split ratio, an effective date, a new CUSIP (the 9-character US security identifier), or whether a bond has been redeemed.
3. **The job today.** Every break must be settled before the 9:30 AM open. The only real tiebreaker is the issuer's own announcement plus the exchange's or SEC's notice, which the analyst finds by hand. That takes an assumed 15 to 25 minutes per break.
4. **The cost of getting it wrong.** A wrong or late fix is expensive:
   - Load a 1-for-25 reverse split one day early, and that day's position is misstated by a factor of 25 in NAV (net asset value) and risk reports.
   - An order on a retired CUSIP rejects at the broker.
   - A redeemed bond stays "live" on the books.
5. **What Break Check does.** It puts both primary sources side by side in seconds, with a citation on every field. Plain code, not an AI model, decides whether they agree, and the analyst still approves every change.

## 2. The workflow today, and the step the applet replaces

1. **Overnight.** The golden-copy build merges Vendor A, Vendor B and the custodian file. Mismatches become exception tickets. *(Unchanged.)*
2. **7:00 AM.** The analyst opens the queue and sorts by impact: held positions first, then pending orders. *(Unchanged.)*
3. **Read the ticket.** The analyst reads both vendor values and the field in dispute. *(Unchanged.)*
4. **Search by hand.** Google, EDGAR and Nasdaq Trader, looking for the issuer's release and the exchange's alert while skipping re-posts and aggregators. **REPLACED:** two Exa calls, one per source type, with domains and a date window set in code.
5. **Read and reconcile.** The analyst reads both documents and works out what each "effective date" means (legal effective time vs first trading day on new terms). **MOSTLY REPLACED:** fields are extracted with a citation each, code compares them field by field and labels known patterns, and the analyst reads the two highlighted sentences to confirm.
6. **Write up.** The analyst pastes links into the ticket and writes a resolution note. **REPLACED:** code drafts the note from the grounded fields and their URLs.
7. **Fix and escalate.** The analyst loads the fix and escalates to whichever vendor was wrong. **Stays human.** The escalation note is drafted, with the evidence attached.
8. **Weeks later.** Audit asks what the firm knew when it loaded the fix. **NEW, optional:** an Exa Snapshot copy of each source as of the ticket's open time.
9. **The case no one catches.** Announced-but-not-yet-effective events (a bond call next month) are found only when a feed changes. **NEW, in production:** a daily early-warning job on held issuers (section 11).

The one step to name on the call: step 4, the manual search, is where the 15 to 25 minutes go. Steps 5 and 6 fall out of it.
